title: Project Overview
description: README.md introduces react-socket-link v1.0: typed WebSocket connection management for React 18+ and standalone TypeScript. It walks through typed protocol definitions with defineSocket, global Provider-based and local hook-based React connections, the React-free /core createSocket API, and options such as heartbeat, reconnect backoff, queueing and codecs. Keep its central idea in mind for the whole tour: a logical connection keeps identity, state, queue and subscriptions while replaceable native WebSockets do the transport.

title: Two Public Entry Points
description: The package exposes two barrels. src/index.ts is the main entry that re-exports everything, core primitives plus the React SocketProvider, registerSocket and hooks, while src/core/index.ts is the React-free '/core' subpath for standalone TypeScript. package.json wires these up as dual ESM/CJS exports with React as an optional peer dependency, so non-React consumers never pull React in.
languageLesson: Barrel files re-export symbols from many modules (export { x } from './y') to form a curated public API. Combined with the package.json 'exports' map, each subpath (e.g. 'react-socket-link/core') becomes a separate, independently importable entry.

title: Typed Socket Definitions
description: ConnectionDefinition.ts is the most depended-upon file in the project: nearly every core and React module imports it. It declares the BaseMessage contract and the SocketDefinition identity/type token, and defineSocket creates frozen, symbol-identified definitions that never open a socket. Separating 'what a socket speaks' from 'a live connection' lets the same definition be reused by the Provider, local hooks and the core API.
languageLesson: A definition object that carries only type parameters (a 'type token' or phantom type) lets TypeScript bind incoming and outgoing message unions to a value at compile time, even though the runtime object holds no messages. Using a unique Symbol for identity means two definitions never collide, even if they look alike.

title: Options, State and Retry Contracts
description: Building on the definitions from Step 3, these contracts describe how a connection is configured and observed. ConnectionOptions.ts defines SocketOptions (heartbeat, reconnect, queue, codec), the default JSON codec and runtime validation/merging; ConnectionState.ts defines status and error-code unions plus immutable ConnectionSnapshot objects; ReconnectionPolicy.ts reduces retry policy to a BackoffStrategy function from attempt number to delay. Backoff.ts supplies the concrete strategies: exponential backoff with full jitter and a fixed delay.
languageLesson: Modelling status and error codes as string-literal union types gives exhaustive checking in switch statements. Representing a strategy as a plain function type, rather than a class hierarchy, keeps the reconnection policy trivially swappable and testable.

title: The Logical Connection
description: LogicalConnection.ts is the heart of the library and pulls together everything from Steps 3 and 4. It is a stable identity that owns the retry policy, outgoing queue, message/state subscriptions and open-waiters, calling validateOptions/mergeOptions, snapshot and exponentialBackoff along the way. It also defines the SocketView (read/send) and SocketController (lifecycle) interfaces and the createSocket factory that both the React layer and /core consumers use.

title: Replaceable WebSocket Transport
description: Underneath each logical connection sits a WebSocketTransport, which wraps a single native WebSocket with an immutable handshake configuration, forwards open/message/error/close events, and manages heartbeat pings and silence timeouts. Because transports are disposable and retired ones never call back, the LogicalConnection from Step 5 can swap them on reconnect or update without leaking stale events. This is the split between logical identity and physical transport that the README promises.

title: SocketProvider and Global Sockets
description: Moving into the React layer, SocketProvider.tsx builds a registry of LogicalConnections from registerSocket registrations, connecting them eagerly on mount and disposing them on unmount in a Strict-Mode-safe way. useGlobalSocket returns the shared read/send SocketView, while useGlobalSocketController returns the full SocketController for connect/reconnect/update/close; both resolve the connection through useProviderSocket. This split keeps ordinary consumers from accidentally driving lifecycle commands on a shared connection.
languageLesson: React context lets a provider share one object (here a registry of connections) with any descendant without prop drilling. In React 18 Strict Mode, development builds mount, unmount and re-mount effects, so cleanup must be idempotent or deferred to avoid destroying a resource that is about to be reused.

title: Component-Scoped Local Sockets
description: useLocalSocket is the alternative to the Provider from Step 7: it calls createSocket to create a connection owned by a single component, connecting on mount and closing/disposing on unmount. Like the Provider, it uses deferred disposal so Strict Mode effect replays do not tear down and recreate the connection. Each hook owner gets an independent logical connection.

title: Event, Send and State Hooks
description: These small hooks work with any socket, global or local. useSocketEvent subscribes a handler to a typed message type (or wildcard) and keeps the latest handler in a ref to avoid resubscribing; useSocketSend returns a memoized send function; useSocketState exposes the ConnectionSnapshot from Step 4 through useSyncExternalStore. Together they turn the LogicalConnection's subscription API into idiomatic React.
languageLesson: useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot) is React 18's tear-free way to read an external mutable store; getSnapshot must return a stable value between changes, which immutable snapshots provide. The 'latest ref' pattern stores a callback in useRef so an effect can call the newest handler without re-running.

title: Test Suite
description: The tests verify the guarantees described so far, backed by MockWebSocket, an EventTarget-based double that records sent payloads and simulates open, message and abnormal-close events. core.test.ts covers identity preservation across transport replacement, update coalescing, backoff, queue bounding, heartbeats and credential redaction; react.test.tsx checks Provider sharing, local socket identity and Strict Mode safety; types.test.ts uses expectTypeOf and @ts-expect-error to lock down the typed protocol from Step 3.
languageLesson: Type-level tests guard generics at compile time: '@ts-expect-error' fails the build if the following line unexpectedly type-checks, and expectTypeOf asserts inferred types, so regressions in message typing surface during typechecking.

title: Build and Tooling
description: vite.config.ts builds the library in library mode with two entries (main index and React-free core) as ES and CJS bundles with React externalized, emits declarations via vite-plugin-dts from tsconfig.build.json, and runs Vitest in jsdom. tsconfig.build.json emits types only for the published sources and excludes tests, while the root tsconfig.json drives editor typechecking across src, tests and configs. This is how the two entry points from Step 2 become the published package.
languageLesson: Externalizing peer dependencies such as React in a library build keeps them out of the bundle, so the consuming app supplies a single copy and avoids duplicate-React hook errors.
